tr.td: Qissa Khwani Bazaar, Peshawar, North-West Frontier Province, British India (now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Pakistan)
Troops and armoured vehicles confronted a crowd protesting the arrest of Khudai Khidmatgar leaders; many demonstrators were killed
20 in official British records; between 200 and 400 in Congress and local estimates; "almost 400" in several modern accounts
Soldiers of the Garhwal Rifles declined to fire on the crowd and were later court-martialled
Khudai Khidmatgar ("Servants of God"), the Red Shirts, founded by Abdul Ghaffar Khan in 1929
Arrest of Abdul Ghaffar Khan and other leaders on 23 April 1930
Civil Disobedience Movement launched by Mahatma Gandhi in March 1930
No 1 Armoured Car Company, lorry-borne infantry, part of a squadron of the Poona Horse (National Army Museum); the Garhwal Rifles
Chandra Singh Garhwali, a Garhwal Rifles havildar
Court martial; sentences of up to eight years according to one source, life imprisonment for Chandra Singh according to another
A Congress enquiry committee (Vithalbhai Patel, per GKToday); a judicial probe under Naimatullah Chaudhry (per The Wire)
Khudai Khidmatgar allied with the Indian National Congress in August 1931

li.a: The Wire (LiveWire): 'San Tees Shaheedan': 91 Years of the Qissa Khwani Bazaar Massacre
Civilsdaily: Qissa Khwani Bazaar massacre and the Khudai Khidmatgars
GS SCORE: Remembering Peshawar's Qissa Khwani Bazaar massacre
Association for India's Development: Chandra Singh Garhwali, a champion that promoted communal harmony during the Indian freedom struggle
Qissa Khwani: The 1930 Civil Disobedience Movement in Peshawar Valley from the Pashtoon Perspective, Part II
National Army Museum, London: Riots in Peshawar, 1930

content.p: On 23 April 1930 the old market street of Peshawar, known as the Qissa Khwani Bazaar or the Market of Storytellers, became the scene of what GKToday calls the first major military confrontation of the Civil Disobedience Movement in the North-West Frontier Province. The authorities had arrested the leaders of the Khudai Khidmatgar, a Pashtun movement pledged to non-violence, and crowds gathered in protest. Armoured cars and troops were called in. Demonstrators were killed in the confrontation, though how many is still disputed: British official records gave 20, while Congress inquiry reports and local sources gave a range of 200 to 400, according to GKToday.

The day is remembered for a second reason too. Indian soldiers of the Royal Garhwal Rifles were reported to have refused an order to fire on the crowd, an act of defiance for which they were court-martialled.

The National Army Museum in London explains the background in terms of the Government of India Act 1919, which began to involve Indians in administration and in self-governing institutions. These reforms were not extended to the North-West Frontier Province, where the museum says the Pathans were considered not yet ready for them. Abdul Ghaffar Khan, whom the museum calls a political agitator, began to rouse the Pathans against this discrimination.

The Wire adds a second grievance. The Frontier Crimes Regulation, it says, denied the province's Pashtun inhabitants the right of appeal, the right to a lawyer and the right to present reasoned evidence. It also describes a deliberate colonial policy: the Pashtuns were classed as a "martial race" and the region kept underdeveloped and without schooling so that it would go on supplying soldiers to the army. Ghaffar Khan, by contrast, saw education as the way to reform Pashtun society and opened a number of "Azad" schools.

Ghaffar Khan founded the Khudai Khidmatgar, which means Servants of God, in 1929. GKToday dates the founding to November of that year. The movement mixed social reform with strict non-violence and opposition to British rule. According to The Wire, members cleaned neighbours' houses and wove their own cloth, and anyone found acting violently was expelled and could be readmitted only after three years of good behaviour. Their red uniforms, which announced their presence instead of hiding it, earned them the name Surkh Posh, or Red Shirts. Civilsdaily says the women of the movement wore black.

The membership was mostly Muslim, but The Wire says Sikhs and Hindus, who were regarded in Pashtun society as hum saya, also joined. The text of the movement's pledge, reproduced in a study of the 1930 events from the Pashtun perspective, committed each volunteer to serve all human beings alike, to help the oppressed against the oppressor, to avoid party feeling and enmity, and not to give security or apologise "during the fight".

The National Army Museum takes a very different view of the movement. It describes the Red Shirts as an unarmed paramilitary body which "drilled openly and preached sedition and violence along the Frontier". The Wire and the other pages treat the group as strictly non-violent, so the sources describe the same movement in opposite terms.

The sources give two accounts of what set off the protest. The Wire says that members of the Indian National Congress came to Peshawar a month after Gandhi's Dandi March to look into the Frontier Crimes Regulation. Hundreds of Khudai Khidmatgar gathered at the railway station to meet them, only to be told that the delegation had been detained in Punjab. According to The Wire, the crowd then threatened to picket liquor shops unless the delegation was released.

GKToday and Civilsdaily give the arrest of Ghaffar Khan as the immediate cause. He was arrested on 23 April 1930, they say, after a speech at Utmanzai, and other Khudai Khidmatgar leaders were arrested at the same time. The National Army Museum says the authorities felt obliged to arrest the movement's leaders at a huge rally in Peshawar, and that the arrests provoked rioting the police could not contain. The Wire says several Pashtun leaders, Ghaffar Khan among them, were arrested on charges of sedition. The pages do not agree on where Ghaffar Khan was taken into custody, and none of them reconciles the Utmanzai speech with the Peshawar rally.

As the protest grew, the police asked for military help. The National Army Museum records that a "City Disturbance Column" was formed from four armoured cars of the No 1 Armoured Car Company, named Bethune, Bray, Bullicourt and Bapaume, with infantry carried in lorries and part of a squadron of the Poona Horse. While the column tried to move through the angry crowds, the museum says, a dispatch rider was killed. The armoured cars stopped to help him and came under attack, and the crew of Bethune fled on foot while the crowd set fire to the motorcyclist and the armoured car. The museum's account stops there and says nothing of the shooting.

The accounts written from the protesters' side start from the same vehicles but describe them differently. GKToday says armoured cars were driven into the dense crowd at high speed and crushed several demonstrators, and that British Indian Army troops then fired machine guns and rifles for several hours while the protesters, bare-chested, stepped forward to replace the fallen. Civilsdaily and GS SCORE give a shorter version: army vehicles drove into the crowd, killing protesters and bystanders, and soldiers then opened fire on unarmed people. The Wire says that when the Khidmatgars were fired on, others came forward to help them, and that they offered to leave the bazaar if they could collect their dead and the troops withdrew; it says the British refused.

The account of the day in the Pashtun-perspective study quotes a narrative that firing went on for hours after the people had dispersed, "in the by-roads, lanes, sub-lanes, balconies and roofs", and calls 23 April "a red day in the Calendar of the Pathans". The same page reproduces verse mourning the dead, in which the bazaar is said to have become a slaughterhouse.

No single figure is agreed. GKToday states that official British colonial records placed the toll at 20, while contemporary Congress inquiry reports and local sources put the toll anywhere from 200 to 400 civilians. The Wire says almost 400 unarmed protesters died, and VisitSilkRoad, a tourism site, says nearly 400 were shot dead. Because those modern pages do not name an original record behind the 400 figure, it is best read as a widely repeated estimate rather than a verified count.
content.h2: The Garhwalis who would not fire
content.p: Several of the pages report that the army tried to use Indian infantry from the Garhwal Rifles against the crowd. Civilsdaily says that, according to historical records, two platoons of the regiment refused to shoot unarmed protesters, and that the British court-martialled the men with sentences of up to eight years. The Wire says the Royal Garhwal Rifles defied orders, and that the whole platoon was arrested and court-martialled. GKToday names the unit as the 2/18th Royal Garhwal Rifles and says that Chandra Singh and 59 fellow soldiers were court-martialled, stripped of rank and given long terms of rigorous imprisonment.

The most detailed story is about Chandra Singh Garhwali, and it comes from a passage that the AID essay quotes from a 1955 biography by the historian Rahul Sankrityayan. In that account, a Captain Ricket told the crowd to disperse or be shot and then ordered the Garhwali soldiers to fire three rounds. Chandra Singh, standing at his left, shouted to the regiment not to fire, and the soldiers of the first and second platoons grounded their rifles. When the captain asked what was wrong, Chandra Singh is quoted as saying: "These people are unarmed. How can be fire on them?" The biography adds that the commander of a third platoon ordered his men to fire and began firing himself, but that his platoon also refused. It says British troops were then sent forward and fired, and that in the resulting turmoil Captain Ricket was killed. This is one author's narrative, relayed by a second writer, and none of the other pages carries the detail about the captain's death.

Not all of the pages place the refusal in the same setting. The AID essay says the British sent the Garhwal regiment to Peshawar and Abbottabad because it was not local, in the hope that its soldiers would crush the protest without hesitation. The account on Uttarakhandi says only that Chandra Singh was sent to Peshawar on 23 April and ordered to attack the protesters, and that he refused.

The punishments are reported differently, and the pages do not make the sentences clear. Uttarakhandi says Chandra Singh and his soldiers were tried, that the barrister Mukundi Lal defended them and that, after persistent efforts, his death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment. It says his property was confiscated and that he was sent to Abbottabad jail for 14 years, though it also says he was released on 26 September 1941 after serving 11 years. GKToday also names Mukandi Lal, a barrister from Lansdowne, as the defence lawyer. AID says the other soldiers faced Kaala Paani, the Andaman and Nicobar prison, and received no recognition after their release.

The Wire says the whole platoon was court-martialled, while Civilsdaily says the men received up to eight years. None of the pages cites a trial record, so the number of men tried and the exact sentences stay unconfirmed.

Two investigations are named, by different pages. GKToday says the Congress set up its own body, the Peshawar Enquiry Committee, under Vithalbhai Patel, and that it went ahead despite British censorship. The Wire says an official probe was ordered, which it attributes to King George VI, and says that a committee led by Naimatullah Chaudhry produced a 200-page report criticising British actions. The pages do not say whether these were two inquiries or one described twice, and neither report is quoted.

GKToday says British forces temporarily lost control of Peshawar for several days and withdrew to the outskirts until reinforced, and that membership of the Khudai Khidmatgar rose from a few hundred to more than 80,000 within months. The Wire likewise says colonial control over Peshawar loosened as protests spread. Civilsdaily says the authorities intensified their crackdown on the movement's leaders and members, and Civilsdaily and GS SCORE say the movement began to involve young women. According to accounts from Khidmatgar activists, those pages say, members suffered harassment, physical violence and religious persecution, and the British tried to divide the province along religious lines.

In August 1931, the pages say, the Khudai Khidmatgar aligned themselves with the Congress. Civilsdaily says this surprised the British and forced them to reduce their violence against the movement. Ghaffar Khan's own judgment, as The Wire quotes it from his autobiography My Life and Struggle, was that a non-violent Pathan was more dangerous to the British than a violent one, so they tried everything to provoke the Khidmatgars into violence and failed.

The later lives of the men and the memory of the day were uneven. The AID essay says Chandra Singh Garhwali died in poverty, and it dates his death to 1 October 1971; Uttarakhandi gives 1 October 1979 and adds that India issued a postage stamp in his honour in 1994. The AID essay adds that in 1954 he wrote to the Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh describing his debts, and that a year later his pension was raised by 14 rupees a month. The writer argues that historians and governments have neglected the Peshawar revolt.

In Pakistan the picture is also one of fading memory. Civilsdaily and GS SCORE both say that after 1947 the Khudai Khidmatgar lost political influence, and that the movement and the massacre have been wiped out of Pakistan's collective memory. Civilsdaily adds that the movement opposed Partition, a stance many read as opposing Pakistan's creation. Today the bazaar is, in the words of VisitSilkRoad, a commercial centre of electronics and clothing shops with narrow alleys and old structures that VisitSilkRoad says still give it a nostalgic look.
